title: Understanding and modelling ammonia partitioning and transport across reverse osmosis membrane

paper_content.abstract:
Reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly applied for the reclamation of ammonia-rich wastewater. However, the
mechanisms governing NH /NH + transport across RO membranes remain unclear. In this study, we develop an
3 4
ammonia partitioning and transport (APT) model to quantitatively describe NH /NH + retention and transport,
3 4
incorporating pH-dependent NH /NH + partitioning and membrane charge variation. The theoretical model is
3 4
validated through laboratory-scale RO experiments under varying pressures, feed concentrations, and pH conditions.
In contrast to stable water permeability, the permeability coefficient of total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is sensitive
to pH value. TAN retention is optimal (89.13.2%) near neutral pH, decreasing at higher pH due to increased NH
3
fraction and at lower pH due to reduced membrane charge. By decoupling diffusion, advection, and
electromigration, the APT model shows distinct NH₄⁺ and NH₃ flux contributions, revealing pH-dependent transport
mechanisms governed by speciation and membrane charge. Molecular dynamics simulations further differentiate
the transport pathways of NH₃ and NH₄⁺, showing that NH
4
+ experiences a significantly higher energy barrier.
Validations with both synthetic and real manure streams demonstrate good predictive accuracy for advancing RO
applications in ammonia-rich streams.
paper_content.introduction:
Ammonia is essential to securing the food supply and supporting global population growth. Synthesized by the
Haber-Bosch process, ammonia has sustained about half of humanity over the past century 1. Currently, the Haber-
Bosch process accounts for 2% of global energy consumption and up to 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions 2-
4. This ammonia is consumed and cycled within the food chain and ends up in the excreta. In the U.S., 60% of
ammonia emissions are attributed to the livestock manure wastewater produced in intensive animal feeding
operations 5. Excess manure nutrients lead to overapplication, increasing nutrient losses and reducing nutrient use
efficiency. The high water content and low nutrient density increase costs to transport manure nutrients to cropland,
with agronomic needs restricting the ability to use manure effectively.

Ammonia in manure can be directly reused through a shortcut resource recovery process 6,7. To achieve clean
water that meets discharge or even drinking standards, anaerobic treatment is applied to livestock manure, followed
by a series of membrane treatment processes 8, to recover energy, nutrients, and clean water out of waste streams.
As the dominant technology for water purification with high energy efficiency, reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly
used for wastewater reclamation 9, particularly for clean water recovery and ammonia concentration 10,11. Compared
with treating the wastewater by nitrification-denitrification and resynthesizing ammonia from the Haber-Bosch
process, this shortcut was estimated to save energy as high as 16.2-19.7 kWh per kg-N 11, making it a more
sustainable solution 12-14.

In practice, it has been found that total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is difficult to fully retain in a single-pass RO,
and thus, a two-pass RO system is often employed to minimize the presence of TAN in the final clean water. Recent
studies reported experimental observation of significant variability in ammonia retention efficiency by RO
membranes, ranging from 0% to 98% 10,11,15,16. These results are particularly sensitive to the operating pH 11. It is
commonly believed that this variability results from the NH /NH + speciation under varying pH, and NH and NH +
3 4 3 4
have their respective permeabilities, which are different from each other. RO membrane is effective for only
rejecting the charged ions, so a high permeability of TAN was observed at alkaline pH, where TAN is mainly in the
form of NH 10,17. However, even at acidic pH where all the TAN exists in the form of NH +,
3 4
its permeability is not
simply a constant due to its interaction with the membrane charge 11. Current understandings are limited to
experimental observations and qualitative descriptions. A fundamental understanding of TAN transport through RO
membranes remains limited; thus, a quantitative model is needed to establish the relation between TAN transport
and pH variation.

Researchers have made significant efforts to develop models to describe the transport of water and salts through
RO membranes 18,19 (Supplementary Table 1). Recent experimental and computational studies demonstrated the
presence of advective transport of solutes within the RO membrane 9,20,21. Correspondingly, advanced models
conceptualizing water and solute transport through porous RO membranes were developed, incorporating more
detailed mechanisms, including Donnan steric partitioning and advective solution friction 22,23. They have shown
improved performance in simulating and fitting data for inert salt ions 24,25. By introducing the fast acid–base
reaction assumption, this modeling framework allows the inclusion of amphoteric ions. Purely simulated results of
pH variation in RO showed the possible feasibility of this modeling framework 26. By adjusting multiple fitting
parameters, reasonable agreement with experiments was achieved when only inert ions and pH were considered 27.
Once additional amphoteric ions (e.g., NH₄⁺) are included, the model’s generalizability declines markedly, and its
predictions of permeate pH, amphoteric ions, and bivalent ions become less reliable even under a single feed pH 28.
The highly coupled and complex equations render the transport of amphoteric ions strongly dependent on the local
membrane pH. For instance, NH₃ transport is governed by the coupled transport of NH₄⁺ and H⁺ 28.

In this study, we propose that the transport of amphoteric ions is governed by uncoupled transport equations of
charged and neutral species, with the solution pH subsequently corrected through equilibrium recalculation. We
analyzed and elucidated the separation and transport of TAN in RO membranes, as well as the complex changes
induced by pH. Based on solute transport theory that considers friction between substances, we developed a
theoretical model, named ammonia partitioning and transport (APT) model, to describe NH /NH + transport in RO
3 4
membranes. This model takes into account diffusion, advection, and electro-migration of solutes, while also
considering the interactions between water, solutes, and the membrane matrix. RO experiments were conducted
under different feed concentrations, pH levels, and operating pressures to validate the model. Our theoretical and
experimental observations reveal the changes in TAN removal performance resulting from the pH-dependent shifts
NH /NH + speciation and RO membrane surface charge, as well as the differences in NH /NH + transmembrane
3 4 3 4
transport behavior, and extend the applicability of the solution-friction model in describing TAN transport in RO
membranes.

We conducted a series of RO experiments to investigate the effects of operating pressure, feed concentration,
and pH on TAN transport to validate the model. The results of varying operating pressure and feed concentration

Impact of pH value on TAN transport
Although previous studies have observed a significant effect of pH on TAN rejection in RO 11,33, no fundamental
explanation has been provided yet. The APT model enables a quantitative description of TAN transport across the
RO membrane, demonstrating a great fitting performance with an R² of 0.956 for TAN permeability (Figure 2b)
and 0.988 for TAN rejection (Figure 2c). The influence of pH values on TAN transport was examined using a bench-
scale RO at a crossflow velocity of 6.2 mm s–1, an operating hydraulic pressure of 10 bar, a feed TAN concentration
of 10.7 mM, and a temperature of 25 ± 1 °C.
We observed stable water permeability independent of feed pH variations. As illustrated in Figure 2a, both
experimental results (0.539  0.019 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) and model calculations (0.554 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) demonstrate a
stable water transport coefficient across the tested feed pH range (5.5 to 11). This is probably because water
transport primarily depends on the frictional interaction between water molecules and the membrane 24. Although
the water transport is theoretically coupled with ion transport, the ion-associated term in Eq. 3 is negligible in dilute
solutions. Therefore, observable changes in water permeability only occur when the membrane properties are
significantly altered, such as by swelling under extreme pH conditions 34 or compaction under excessively high
pressure 35.
TAN permeability coefficient initially decreases slightly as feed pH increases, followed by a sharp increase
when the pH exceeds 8 (Figure 2b). The model results indicate that the lowest permeability coefficient occurs at
pH 7.3, with a value of 0.656 L m⁻² h⁻¹. Correspondingly, TAN rejection exhibits a parabolic trend (Figure 2c),
with the highest experimental rejection of 89.13.2% observed near pH 7 and a model-predicted maximum of 88.7%
at pH 7.3. Both high and low pH levels in the feed solution led to a reduced TAN rejection efficiency. This arch-
shaped behavior has also been reported in previous studies 11,36. To better understand the arch-shape, we use the
APT model to separate the pH-dependent transport behavior of TAN into individual transport characteristics of
NH₃ and NH₄⁺.
NH₃ permeability remains constant across the feed pH range of 5.5 to 11, with a value of 24.75 L m⁻² h⁻¹ (Figure
2b). As a result, its rejection remains consistently low at 17.2% (Figure 2b). This is because NH₃ is uncharged and
therefore does not interact with the membrane charge. However, the NH₃ transport flux increased from 0.00851
mmol m⁻² h⁻¹ to 44.7 mmol m⁻² h⁻¹ when the feed pH value varied from 5.5 to 10.4 (Figure 2d). This results from
the pH-dependent distribution of NH₃ and NH₄⁺. Given that the permeability of NH₃ is approximately 30 times
higher than that of NH₄⁺, an increase in NH₃ fraction at high feed pH significantly boosts overall TAN permeability
and reduces rejection efficiency.
NH₄⁺ permeability slightly decreases from 1.18 L m⁻² h⁻¹ to 0.21 L m⁻² h⁻¹ as feed pH increases from 5.5 to 11,
respectively. As shown in the inset of Figure 2b, there are two distinct drops for NH + permeability, one at a feed

In addition to total TAN concentration and the NH₃/NH₄⁺ speciation (Figure 2e), the APT model also accurately
predicts permeate pH values, showing good agreement with experimental results (R2 = 0.973, Figure 2f). Notably,
the permeate pH is constantly higher than the feed pH. For instance, with a feed pH of 8.45, the permeate pH

paper_content.methods:
Model development
The commercial RO membranes typically use the thin-film composite polyamide membranes produced through
interfacial polymerization 42. The model in this study describes the membrane layer as a polymer network with
continuous, water-filled sub-nanometer channels through which clusters of water molecules and solutes can move
24. The support layer also has a similar polymer network, but with much larger voids, and thus, its effect on water
and solute transport can be neglected during model development, allowing us to focus only on the active layer of
the membrane. In the polymer matrix of the membrane, water exists in a liquid phase, while solutes are dispersed
in the water and transported across the membrane through the aqueous phase.
Previous modeling strategies for the transmembrane transport of amphoteric ions were commonly based on the
assumption of infinitely fast acid-base equilibrations 43, treating amphoteric ions as a group and establishing their
relationship through dissociation equilibrium at every local point inside the membrane 28. However, such method
cannot describe the transport mechanism of NH as its concentration was calculated based on the transport of NH +
3 4
and local pH instead of its own governing equation. To address this, we established individual transport equations
for both NH + and NH according to their respective transport mechanisms (Eqs 1.1-2.2). For simplification, we

within the pH range we care about 43, otherwise their involvement would introduce more equations than unknowns

dissociation equilibrium between the transported NH and NH +. Their distribution in solution is determined by the

Equation solving and parameter fitting procedure
The model is solved analytically following a structured two-loop procedure. The outer loop iterates over
experimental conditions investigated in this study, including feed pH, solute concentration, or permeate flux. Under
each fixed condition, an inner loop determines whether the concentration polarization condition (Eq. 6) is satisfied.
At the beginning of each iteration, the solute concentration at the membrane surface is assumed equal to that in the
feed (i.e., c = c , no polarization).
s f
At the feed-side membrane-water interface, the Donnan-steric partition equations (Eqs. 1.1 and 1.2), together
with the electroneutrality condition inside the membrane (Eqs. 8 and 10), form a solvable system that yields the
solute concentrations and the dimensionless potential difference (∆𝜑 ) at the interface. Within the membrane,
transport equations (Eqs. 2.1 and 2.2) are constructed, which, together with Eqs. (7) (8) and (10), form another
solvable system. This system yields the concentrations and potential difference at the permeate-side interior of the
membrane. At the permeate-side membrane-water interface, the Donnan-steric equilibrium conditions (Eqs. 1.1 and
1.2), coupled with Eqs. (8) (9) and (10), provide analytical solutions for the permeate concentrations of all solutes.
The resulting permeate concentrations (c ) are then substituted back into Eq. (6) to compute the membrane
p
surface concentrations that satisfy the concentration polarization condition. If the updated values differ from the
initial guess, the membrane-surface concentrations are updated by averaging the new and old values; the process
iterates until concentrations at the feed, membrane surface, and permeate simultaneously satisfy Eq. (6). At
convergence, the solution set satisfies all coupled relationships, including concentration polarization, Donnan and
steric partitioning, and Nernst–Planck transport. Because NH₃ and NH₄⁺ exhibit different permeabilities, they must
reestablish chemical equilibrium via Eq. (5), which determines the permeate pH. After obtaining solute
concentrations and fluxes, the pressure drop across the membrane is determined through Eqs. (3), (13), and (14).
Parameter fitting was performed by minimizing the discrepancies between measured and calculated values. The
partitioning coefficients were fitted by minimizing the sum of squared errors between measured and predicted TAN
permeability coefficient and the rejection, with a weighing factor to adjust their magnitude to be the same level,
while the fluid–membrane friction parameter was fitted using water permeability measurements. Optimization was
conducted in MATLAB using the ‘fminsearch’ function (Nelder–Mead algorithm). To enhance convergence and
reduce the likelihood of local minima, the partitioning coefficients were constrained to the literature-based range
of 0–0.2 24,28, and the friction parameter was searched within a logarithmic range of 1013–1017. A multi-start strategy
(n = 4) was applied to further reduce the risk of local minima. Minor manual adjustments were applied to ensure a
consistent parameter set across multiple operating conditions (e.g., varying feed pH, operating pressures, and feed
concentrations; Supplementary Figures 1–2). A complete list of parameter values and their origins (literature-based,
experimentally determined, or fitted) is provided in Supplementary Table 2.

Chemicals and Materials
Lab-scale RO experiments were conducted using both synthetic NH Cl solution and real anaerobic effluent from
4
a dairy farm. The synthetic NH Cl solution was prepared by dissolving reagent grade ammonium chloride
4
(Laboratory Grade, Ward’s Science, Rochester, NY) in deionized water. A 1 M NaOH solution and a 1 M HCl
solution were used to adjust the pH of the RO feed. The real wastewater was collected from a dairy farm located in
northern Wisconsin (4439’37.6”N, 8735’15.1”W), where the manure wastewater had been anaerobically digested
and processed by a series of membrane treatments. The wastewater was from the effluent of UF and 1st pass RO,
respectively, which served as the feed for the following 1st pass and 2nd pass RO, respectively. Detailed chemical
information about the water is provided in Supplementary Table 3. The membrane used in the RO setup was a
commercial polyamide thin-film composite RO membrane (BW3E0, Dow Filmtec), purchased from Sterlitech
Corporation (Auburn, WA), designed for brackish water desalination with low pressure requirements. The received
membranes were stored in the dark at 4°C.

RO Setup and Experiments
A bench-scale crossflow RO system (Innovator CF016, Sterlitech Corporation, Auburn, WA) was employed to
carry out the RO experiment. The system featured a rectangular plate-and-frame feed flow channel with dimensions
of 5.3 cm in length, 3.9 cm in width, and 0.23 cm in depth, giving it an active membrane area of 20.6 cm2. A porous
stainless-steel frit provided mechanical support on the permeate side.
All experiments were conducted at 25 ± 1°C, with a crossflow velocity of 6.2 mm s⁻¹ at the membrane surface.
The retentate was recirculated back to the feed tank, and experiments were conducted across a range of operating
pressures from 5 to 20 bar, feed TAN concentrations from 50 to 1270 mg N/L, and feed pH values from 5.5 to 10.5
to determine TAN rejection rates and permeate flux. The feed volume for each experimental condition was 2 L.
Newly installed membranes in the RO system were first equilibrated with deionized water for 5 hours at the
experimental operating pressure. Subsequently, the membranes were equilibrated with the feed solution under
experimental conditions for 30 minutes before permeate samples were collected. The permeate reservoir was placed
on an electronic balance (Scout SPX2201, OHAUS, Pine Brook, NJ) to continuously monitor permeate flux by
tracking weight changes. The volume of permeate collected during the experiment did not exceed 2% of the total
feed volume, allowing us to assume that the composition of the solution in the feed tank remained unchanged. The
TAN, chemical oxygen demand, and total nitrogen were measured using the Nitrogen-Ammonia Reagent Set HR,
the COD Digestion Vials HR, and the Total Nitrogen Reagent Set HR (Hach, Loveland, CO), respectively, with a
spectrophotometer (DR900, Hach, Loveland, CO). The individual concentrations of NH and NH + were calculated
3 4
using Eq. (1). The cation composition of the real wastewater was determined by inductively coupled plasma optical
emission spectrometry (5800 VDV ICP-OES, Agilent, Santa Clara, CA), while the anion composition was
measured using ion chromatography (IC, Thermo Dionex 2100, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Repeated
experiments were conducted with different membrane samples cut from the same sheet under identical experimental
conditions to minimize errors due to membrane variability.

Molecular dynamics simulation
Membrane preparation. Reverse-osmosis polyamide membrane with dimensions of 4.7×4.7×9 nm3 was
prepared with MPD and TMC as described in our previous work 53. Monomers MPD and TMC were placed
randomly inside a box, maintaining a target density of 1.3 g cm–3 and MPD:TMC ratio of 1.5. The initial system
was energy-minimized using the steepest-descent method, followed by crosslinking reactions at 300 K using a
canonical ensemble. During crosslinking, reactive sites within a cutoff distance of 0.45 nm were pulled towards
each other using virtual elastic springs. As the distance between reactive sites decreased below 0.15 nm, the
topologies were updated by adding amide bonds and removing appropriate H and Cl atoms. The crosslinking steps

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript described an ammonia nitrogen partitioning and transport (ANPT) model to predict NH3/NH4+ transport in RO membranes. This model takes into account diffusion, advection, and electro-migration of solutes, while also considering the interactions between water, solutes, and the membrane matrix. This model seems to be useful framework for predicting the transport and rejection of NH3/NH4+ in RO membrane, which is important study for resource recovery. However, the operating conditions examined in this paper appear to be at a gap with regard to their application towards the intended ammonia recovery and reuse. There are some questions remain regarding the points indicated below.
1. This paper mentioned that it aims to understand the mechanisms of the transport of NH3/NH4+ across RO membranes especially in ammonia-rich streams. However, TAN concentrations have only been investigated within the range of a few tens of mM (such as Figure S2). This is because the present study focuses on manure stream under conditions where ammonia concentration and other ions are dilute. If this model is to be considered universally applicable for ammonia recovery from the various wastewater, it is thought that tests should be conducted at higher pressures (up to 70 bar) and with higher concentrations of ammonia. Is this model unable to deal with the 2nd RO shown in Fig. 5a? For example, other research paper presented a high NH4+ concentration of the industrial wastewater by osmotically assisted RO process over 40,000 ppm of total N using cellulose triacetate membranes (Sep. Purif. Technol, 352, 128159, 2025). Therefore, it is necessary to demonstrate the maximum concentration levels this model can predict. As it stands, the model is only applicable under limited conditions.
2. Similarly to Question 1, what is the effect of other types and concentrations of coexisting ions on this model? In the authentic wastewater shown in Table S2, all other ions are either close to zero or, at most, in the tens of mg/L order of magnitude. Consequently, these other ions appear to exert negligible influence on the model, likely contributing to the good fitting results observed in Fig. 5. What effects might be expected on this model under conditions where other ion concentrations are high? Such investigations are thought to yield good predictions for actual wastewater.
3. In the MD simulation of Fig.4, the authors mentioned that “adsorption of NH4+ is mainly dictated by electrostatic attraction with the polyamide membrane, while NH3 is not.” Please compare the extent to which electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces influence the interaction between NH₄⁺ or NH₃ with polyamide membranes.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript develops an Ammonia Nitrogen Partitioning and Transport (ANPT) model for RO that couples steric, Donnan, dielectric partitioning at the interfaces with extended Nernst-Planck/Maxwell-Stefan transport inside the membrane, and explicitly treats NH3 and NH4+ as separate species with re‑equilibration in the permeate. Bench‑scale RO experiments across pressure, TAN concentration, and pH validate the model. MD simulations further show higher free‑energy barriers for NH4+ than NH3, indirectly corroborating the observed phenomena. The model also performs well on an authentic manure RO effluent. The topic is timely and the integration of modeling with experiments and MD is attractive, but several major issues require clarification and improvement. Below are the specific comments.
1. Literature survey on modeling attempts is insufficient. The Introduction cites foundational RO transport studies and some recent advances, but it lacks a cohesive, critical survey of modeling frameworks directly comparable to ANPT such as other Maxwell-Stefan variants, pH‑coupled or amphoteric‑ion transport models. Please add a section that (i) maps the assumptions, governing equations, and capabilities of prior models to those of ANPT; (ii) identifies what is novel here; and (iii) explains when ANPT reduces to or diverges from earlier models. A compact comparison table would help readers position your contribution. The current manuscript gives only hints at these ideas but does not synthesize the overarching modeling framework.
2. Lines 167-172 and 209-213: These sections appear contradictory. The first states that counter ion transport is reduced at high pH, whereas the second says NH4+ partition increases at high pH. Please revise these passages for clarity, as they describe key findings of the paper.
3. You state that partitioning coefficients and the fluid-membrane friction (f_f-m) were fitted, with other parameters set to “typical values.” Please (i) describe the fitting protocol (objective function, optimizer, constraints); (ii) report confidence intervals; and (iii) discuss the possibility of multiple optimal solutions. In addition, a global sensitivity analysis on Φ_i, K_a,i/K_d,i, ε, L_m, and k would quantify robustness of conclusions. Table S1 lists many fixed quantities; please indicate which were literature-based (with sources) and which were fitted.
4. The feed‑side mass‑transfer coefficient k is computed from a Sherwood correlation using an average diffusion coefficient. Please (i) justify the single‑D approach for a multi‑solute, pH‑dependent system, (why not individual k values coupled with the electroneutrality?); (ii) show sensitivity of predictions to k; and (iii) report the film Péclet numbers used. Because CP directly affects surface concentrations, a quantitative CP analysis is important for the pressure and feed concentration sweeps.
5. The model treats NH3 and NH4+ separately and re‑establishes equilibrium only in the permeate, omitting explicit H+/OH- transport under a “thin membrane/fast transport” assumption in Methods. Please justify this choice and if possible, test sensitivity under finite rate NH3 <--> NH4+ scenarios inside the membrane to assess its effect on predicted permeate pH.
6. The system of equations is nonlinear and implicit. Please describe the numerical schemes used and boundary conditions especially for Donnan potentials and concentration polarization. Also clarify whether activity coefficients were assumed to be unity and discuss implications.
7. The MD results showing higher energy barriers for NH4+ than NH3 are valuable. To strengthen the link to ANPT, discuss how these barriers relate to effective partitioning/permeability in the continuum model. Also comment on sensitivity to degree of crosslinking and charge density (the authors simulate 90% crosslinking and two charge states) and then quantify uncertainty in effective energy barrier.
8. The real permeate used for the second RO pass has moderate conductivity and relatively simple ion composition. Please clarify (i) variability across samples; (ii) potential fouling or compaction effects; and (iii) how ANPT could extend to higher TDS or multivalent rich feeds. A brief discussion of limits of applicability would help practitioners.
Minor comments:
- State how Figure 1a was obtained via equilibrium calculations or from literature data.
- Define all velocity terms (v_f, v_m, v_i).
- Ensure every result statement refers to the correct figure (e.g., when discussing fitting performance near Line 140, reference the corresponding figure).
- Standardize units (L based permeability while mmol based fluxes). Using volumetric units may be confusing. Consider expressing results in molar or mass units.
- Indicate n for replicates in all figure captions and include consistent error bars.
- Adding an identity line (y=x) would be helpful in Figure 2f.
- Use TAN consistently (rather than alternating with “AN”)
- Consider including comparative results from previous studies for flux components (advection, diffusion, electromigration).
- In Figure 4a, include a labeled coordinate system.
- Present the key model equations together in the main text for clarity, rather than splitting them across the main text and SI.
- The opening section on global food demand and ammonia’s role is informative but lengthy. It could be shortened to focus more on the modeling novelty and knowledge gap.
- Specify spacer geometry used to justify the Sherwood correlation and list physical properties (Re, Sc) used.
- Describe other experimental conditions (UF pretreatment, volumetric flow, etc.) where relevant.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript addresses modeling approaches to simulate the transport of ammonia nitrogen species through RO membranes. The topic is interesting and relevant. However, I identified several major issues throughout the paper that must be addressed before further consideration.
At its current stage, the manuscript and its results do not convincingly support the proposed results and conclusions, leaving substantial doubts about the robustness and originality of the work.
Major Comments
1. The "Introduction" part in Main reads very similarly to previously published papers, particularly in structure and flow, with only minor changes in content. Please clarify the novelty and clearly distinguish this work from earlier studies.
2. The terminology alternates between TAN and AN throughout the manuscript, which is confusing. Please standardize the notation consistently.
3. How are concentration gradients at the boundary layers considered in Eqs. (1.1) and (1.2)? Which term(s) represent concentration polarization?
4. Please include units for all parameters when they are first introduced. For example, indicate the unit of concentration (e.g., mmol/L) in Eqs. (1.1)–(3).
5. Line 119: Is the coordinate, x, dimensionless or dimensional? If nondimensionalized, please clarify and show the scaling.
6. Lines 153–154 discuss permeability but use the unit of flux (L/m2/h), particularly for TAN. Please check for consistency, including Figure 2b.
7. Why was the model validation (Figure 2) performed only within the pH range of 6–10? Since many RO systems operate under slightly acidic conditions, expanding this range would strengthen the applicability of the model.
8. How were NH3 and NH4+ concentrations in the permeate determined separately? If these were calculated rather than directly measured (as suggested in the Methods), please specify this in the figure captions. Also clarify how pH was measured—especially for the permeate.
9. Figure 3a differentiates fluxes by mechanism. Are there experimental results that support this separation?
10. Lines 190–235 describe possible removal mechanisms qualitatively, but without quantitative analysis. Since the paper claims to provide mechanistic insight into TAN removal, more rigorous quantification is needed.
11. Figure 4 and its corresponding discussion are unclear. Do the simulations account for factors such as concentration gradients, surface charge effects, or other transport parameters? Please specify what variables were included, especially for Figures 4a and 4b.
12. The validation with real wastewater appears to involve only a single sample (Table S2). If so, it may not be sufficient to generalize the model’s applicability or predictability.
13. Long-term operation could lead to fouling and changes in surface charge, affecting TAN transport and rejection. Please discuss how these potential effects may influence the model and its applicability.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly applied for the reclamation of ammonia-rich wastewater. However, the
mechanisms governing NH /NH + transport across RO membranes remain unclear. In this study, we develop an
3 4
ammonia partitioning and transport (APT) model to quantitatively describe NH /NH + retention and transport,
3 4
incorporating pH-dependent NH /NH + partitioning and membrane charge variation. The theoretical model is
3 4
validated through laboratory-scale RO experiments under varying pressures, feed concentrations, and pH conditions.
In contrast to stable water permeability, the permeability coefficient of total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is sensitive
to pH value. TAN retention is optimal (89.13.2%) near neutral pH, decreasing at higher pH due to increased NH
3
fraction and at lower pH due to reduced membrane charge. By decoupling diffusion, advection, and
electromigration, the APT model shows distinct NH₄⁺ and NH₃ flux contributions, revealing pH-dependent transport
mechanisms governed by speciation and membrane charge. Molecular dynamics simulations further differentiate
the transport pathways of NH₃ and NH₄⁺, showing that NH
4
+ experiences a significantly higher energy barrier.
Validations with both synthetic and real manure streams demonstrate good predictive accuracy for advancing RO
applications in ammonia-rich streams.

---

## Introduction

Ammonia is essential to securing the food supply and supporting global population growth. Synthesized by the
Haber-Bosch process, ammonia has sustained about half of humanity over the past century 1. Currently, the Haber-
Bosch process accounts for 2% of global energy consumption and up to 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions 2-
4. This ammonia is consumed and cycled within the food chain and ends up in the excreta. In the U.S., 60% of
ammonia emissions are attributed to the livestock manure wastewater produced in intensive animal feeding
operations 5. Excess manure nutrients lead to overapplication, increasing nutrient losses and reducing nutrient use
efficiency. The high water content and low nutrient density increase costs to transport manure nutrients to cropland,
with agronomic needs restricting the ability to use manure effectively.

Ammonia in manure can be directly reused through a shortcut resource recovery process 6,7. To achieve clean
water that meets discharge or even drinking standards, anaerobic treatment is applied to livestock manure, followed
by a series of membrane treatment processes 8, to recover energy, nutrients, and clean water out of waste streams.
As the dominant technology for water purification with high energy efficiency, reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly
used for wastewater reclamation 9, particularly for clean water recovery and ammonia concentration 10,11. Compared
with treating the wastewater by nitrification-denitrification and resynthesizing ammonia from the Haber-Bosch
process, this shortcut was estimated to save energy as high as 16.2-19.7 kWh per kg-N 11, making it a more
sustainable solution 12-14.

In practice, it has been found that total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is difficult to fully retain in a single-pass RO,
and thus, a two-pass RO system is often employed to minimize the presence of TAN in the final clean water. Recent
studies reported experimental observation of significant variability in ammonia retention efficiency by RO
membranes, ranging from 0% to 98% 10,11,15,16. These results are particularly sensitive to the operating pH 11. It is
commonly believed that this variability results from the NH /NH + speciation under varying pH, and NH and NH +
3 4 3 4
have their respective permeabilities, which are different from each other. RO membrane is effective for only
rejecting the charged ions, so a high permeability of TAN was observed at alkaline pH, where TAN is mainly in the
form of NH 10,17. However, even at acidic pH where all the TAN exists in the form of NH +,
3 4
its permeability is not
simply a constant due to its interaction with the membrane charge 11. Current understandings are limited to
experimental observations and qualitative descriptions. A fundamental understanding of TAN transport through RO
membranes remains limited; thus, a quantitative model is needed to establish the relation between TAN transport
and pH variation.

Researchers have made significant efforts to develop models to describe the transport of water and salts through
RO membranes 18,19 (Supplementary Table 1). Recent experimental and computational studies demonstrated the
presence of advective transport of solutes within the RO membrane 9,20,21. Correspondingly, advanced models
conceptualizing water and solute transport through porous RO membranes were developed, incorporating more
detailed mechanisms, including Donnan steric partitioning and advective solution friction 22,23. They have shown
improved performance in simulating and fitting data for inert salt ions 24,25. By introducing the fast acid–base
reaction assumption, this modeling framework allows the inclusion of amphoteric ions. Purely simulated results of
pH variation in RO showed the possible feasibility of this modeling framework 26. By adjusting multiple fitting
parameters, reasonable agreement with experiments was achieved when only inert ions and pH were considered 27.
Once additional amphoteric ions (e.g., NH₄⁺) are included, the model’s generalizability declines markedly, and its
predictions of permeate pH, amphoteric ions, and bivalent ions become less reliable even under a single feed pH 28.
The highly coupled and complex equations render the transport of amphoteric ions strongly dependent on the local
membrane pH. For instance, NH₃ transport is governed by the coupled transport of NH₄⁺ and H⁺ 28.

In this study, we propose that the transport of amphoteric ions is governed by uncoupled transport equations of
charged and neutral species, with the solution pH subsequently corrected through equilibrium recalculation. We
analyzed and elucidated the separation and transport of TAN in RO membranes, as well as the complex changes
induced by pH. Based on solute transport theory that considers friction between substances, we developed a
theoretical model, named ammonia partitioning and transport (APT) model, to describe NH /NH + transport in RO
3 4
membranes. This model takes into account diffusion, advection, and electro-migration of solutes, while also
considering the interactions between water, solutes, and the membrane matrix. RO experiments were conducted
under different feed concentrations, pH levels, and operating pressures to validate the model. Our theoretical and
experimental observations reveal the changes in TAN removal performance resulting from the pH-dependent shifts
NH /NH + speciation and RO membrane surface charge, as well as the differences in NH /NH + transmembrane
3 4 3 4
transport behavior, and extend the applicability of the solution-friction model in describing TAN transport in RO
membranes.

Impact of pH value on TAN transport
Although previous studies have observed a significant effect of pH on TAN rejection in RO 11,33, no fundamental
explanation has been provided yet. The APT model enables a quantitative description of TAN transport across the
RO membrane, demonstrating a great fitting performance with an R² of 0.956 for TAN permeability (Figure 2b)
and 0.988 for TAN rejection (Figure 2c). The influence of pH values on TAN transport was examined using a bench-
scale RO at a crossflow velocity of 6.2 mm s–1, an operating hydraulic pressure of 10 bar, a feed TAN concentration
of 10.7 mM, and a temperature of 25 ± 1 °C.
We observed stable water permeability independent of feed pH variations. As illustrated in Figure 2a, both
experimental results (0.539  0.019 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) and model calculations (0.554 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) demonstrate a
stable water transport coefficient across the tested feed pH range (5.5 to 11). This is probably because water
transport primarily depends on the frictional interaction between water molecules and the membrane 24. Although
the water transport is theoretically coupled with ion transport, the ion-associated term in Eq. 3 is negligible in dilute
solutions. Therefore, observable changes in water permeability only occur when the membrane properties are
significantly altered, such as by swelling under extreme pH conditions 34 or compaction under excessively high
pressure 35.
TAN permeability coefficient initially decreases slightly as feed pH increases, followed by a sharp increase
when the pH exceeds 8 (Figure 2b). The model results indicate that the lowest permeability coefficient occurs at
pH 7.3, with a value of 0.656 L m⁻² h⁻¹. Correspondingly, TAN rejection exhibits a parabolic trend (Figure 2c),

at pH 7.3. Both high and low pH levels in the feed solution led to a reduced TAN rejection efficiency. This arch-

## Methods

Model development
The commercial RO membranes typically use the thin-film composite polyamide membranes produced through
interfacial polymerization 42. The model in this study describes the membrane layer as a polymer network with
continuous, water-filled sub-nanometer channels through which clusters of water molecules and solutes can move
24. The support layer also has a similar polymer network, but with much larger voids, and thus, its effect on water
and solute transport can be neglected during model development, allowing us to focus only on the active layer of
the membrane. In the polymer matrix of the membrane, water exists in a liquid phase, while solutes are dispersed
in the water and transported across the membrane through the aqueous phase.
Previous modeling strategies for the transmembrane transport of amphoteric ions were commonly based on the
assumption of infinitely fast acid-base equilibrations 43, treating amphoteric ions as a group and establishing their
relationship through dissociation equilibrium at every local point inside the membrane 28. However, such method
cannot describe the transport mechanism of NH as its concentration was calculated based on the transport of NH +
3 4
and local pH instead of its own governing equation. To address this, we established individual transport equations
for both NH + and NH according to their respective transport mechanisms (Eqs 1.1-2.2). For simplification, we
4 3

within the pH range we care about 43, otherwise their involvement would introduce more equations than unknowns
in the coupled system, leading to conflicts of solving. The permeate pH is determined by the re-established
dissociation equilibrium between the transported NH and NH +. Their distribution in solution is determined by the

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript described an ammonia nitrogen partitioning and transport (ANPT) model to predict NH3/NH4+ transport in RO membranes. This model takes into account diffusion, advection, and electro-migration of solutes, while also considering the interactions between water, solutes, and the membrane matrix. This model seems to be useful framework for predicting the transport and rejection of NH3/NH4+ in RO membrane, which is important study for resource recovery. However, the operating conditions examined in this paper appear to be at a gap with regard to their application towards the intended ammonia recovery and reuse. There are some questions remain regarding the points indicated below.
1. This paper mentioned that it aims to understand the mechanisms of the transport of NH3/NH4+ across RO membranes especially in ammonia-rich streams. However, TAN concentrations have only been investigated within the range of a few tens of mM (such as Figure S2). This is because the present study focuses on manure stream under conditions where ammonia concentration and other ions are dilute. If this model is to be considered universally applicable for ammonia recovery from the various wastewater, it is thought that tests should be conducted at higher pressures (up to 70 bar) and with higher concentrations of ammonia. Is this model unable to deal with the 2nd RO shown in Fig. 5a? For example, other research paper presented a high NH4+ concentration of the industrial wastewater by osmotically assisted RO process over 40,000 ppm of total N using cellulose triacetate membranes (Sep. Purif. Technol, 352, 128159, 2025). Therefore, it is necessary to demonstrate the maximum concentration levels this model can predict. As it stands, the model is only applicable under limited conditions.
2. Similarly to Question 1, what is the effect of other types and concentrations of coexisting ions on this model? In the authentic wastewater shown in Table S2, all other ions are either close to zero or, at most, in the tens of mg/L order of magnitude. Consequently, these other ions appear to exert negligible influence on the model, likely contributing to the good fitting results observed in Fig. 5. What effects might be expected on this model under conditions where other ion concentrations are high? Such investigations are thought to yield good predictions for actual wastewater.
3. In the MD simulation of Fig.4, the authors mentioned that “adsorption of NH4+ is mainly dictated by electrostatic attraction with the polyamide membrane, while NH3 is not.” Please compare the extent to which electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces influence the interaction between NH₄⁺ or NH₃ with polyamide membranes.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript develops an Ammonia Nitrogen Partitioning and Transport (ANPT) model for RO that couples steric, Donnan, dielectric partitioning at the interfaces with extended Nernst-Planck/Maxwell-Stefan transport inside the membrane, and explicitly treats NH3 and NH4+ as separate species with re‑equilibration in the permeate. Bench‑scale RO experiments across pressure, TAN concentration, and pH validate the model. MD simulations further show higher free‑energy barriers for NH4+ than NH3, indirectly corroborating the observed phenomena. The model also performs well on an authentic manure RO effluent. The topic is timely and the integration of modeling with experiments and MD is attractive, but several major issues require clarification and improvement. Below are the specific comments.
1. Literature survey on modeling attempts is insufficient. The Introduction cites foundational RO transport studies and some recent advances, but it lacks a cohesive, critical survey of modeling frameworks directly comparable to ANPT such as other Maxwell-Stefan variants, pH‑coupled or amphoteric‑ion transport models. Please add a section that (i) maps the assumptions, governing equations, and capabilities of prior models to those of ANPT; (ii) identifies what is novel here; and (iii) explains when ANPT reduces to or diverges from earlier models. A compact comparison table would help readers position your contribution. The current manuscript gives only hints at these ideas but does not synthesize the overarching modeling framework.
2. Lines 167-172 and 209-213: These sections appear contradictory. The first states that counter ion transport is reduced at high pH, whereas the second says NH4+ partition increases at high pH. Please revise these passages for clarity, as they describe key findings of the paper.

You state that partitioning coefficients and the fluid-membrane friction (f_f-m) were fitted, with other parameters set to “typical values.” Please (i) describe the fitting protocol (objective function, optimizer, constraints); (ii) report confidence intervals; and (iii) discuss the possibility of multiple optimal solutions. In addition, a global sensitivity analysis on Φ_i, K_a,i/K_d,i, ε, L_m, and k would quantify robustness of conclusions. ## Abstract

Reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly applied for the reclamation of ammonia-rich wastewater. However, the
mechanisms governing NH /NH + transport across RO membranes remain unclear. In this study, we develop an
3 4
ammonia partitioning and transport (APT) model to quantitatively describe NH /NH + retention and transport,
3 4
incorporating pH-dependent NH /NH + partitioning and membrane charge variation. The theoretical model is
3 4
validated through laboratory-scale RO experiments under varying pressures, feed concentrations, and pH conditions.
In contrast to stable water permeability, the permeability coefficient of total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is sensitive
to pH value. TAN retention is optimal (89.13.2%) near neutral pH, decreasing at higher pH due to increased NH
3
fraction and at lower pH due to reduced membrane charge. By decoupling diffusion, advection, and
electromigration, the APT model shows distinct NH₄⁺ and NH₃ flux contributions, revealing pH-dependent transport
mechanisms governed by speciation and membrane charge. Molecular dynamics simulations further differentiate
the transport pathways of NH₃ and NH₄⁺, showing that NH
4

Validations with both synthetic and real manure streams demonstrate good predictive accuracy for advancing RO
applications in ammonia-rich streams.

## Introduction

Ammonia is essential to securing the food supply and supporting global population growth. Synthesized by the
Haber-Bosch process, ammonia has sustained about half of humanity over the past century 1. Currently, the Haber-
Bosch process accounts for 2% of global energy consumption and up to 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions 2-
4. This ammonia is consumed and cycled within the food chain and ends up in the excreta. In the U.S., 60% of
ammonia emissions are attributed to the livestock manure wastewater produced in intensive animal feeding
operations 5. Excess manure nutrients lead to overapplication, increasing nutrient losses and reducing nutrient use
efficiency. The high water content and low nutrient density increase costs to transport manure nutrients to cropland,
with agronomic needs restricting the ability to use manure effectively.

Ammonia in manure can be directly reused through a shortcut resource recovery process 6,7. To achieve clean
water that meets discharge or even drinking standards, anaerobic treatment is applied to livestock manure, followed
by a series of membrane treatment processes 8, to recover energy, nutrients, and clean water out of waste streams.
As the dominant technology for water purification with high energy efficiency, reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly
used for wastewater reclamation 9, particularly for clean water recovery and ammonia concentration 10,11. Compared
with treating the wastewater by nitrification-denitrification and resynthesizing ammonia from the Haber-Bosch
process, this shortcut was estimated to save energy as high as 16.2-19.7 kWh per kg-N 11, making it a more
sustainable solution 12-14.

In practice, it has been found that total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is difficult to fully retain in a single-pass RO,
and thus, a two-pass RO system is often employed to minimize the presence of TAN in the final clean water. Recent
studies reported experimental observation of significant variability in ammonia retention efficiency by RO
membranes, ranging from 0% to 98% 10,11,15,16. These results are particularly sensitive to the operating pH 11. It is
commonly believed that this variability results from the NH /NH + speciation under varying pH, and NH and NH +
3 4 3 4
have their respective permeabilities, which are different from each other. RO membrane is effective for only
rejecting the charged ions, so a high permeability of TAN was observed at alkaline pH, where TAN is mainly in the
form of NH 10,17. However, even at acidic pH where all the TAN exists in the form of NH +,
3 4
its permeability is not
simply a constant due to its interaction with the membrane charge 11. Current understandings are limited to
experimental observations and qualitative descriptions. A fundamental understanding of TAN transport through RO
membranes remains limited; thus, a quantitative model is needed to establish the relation between TAN transport
and pH variation.

Researchers have made significant efforts to develop models to describe the transport of water and salts through
RO membranes 18,19 (Supplementary Table 1). Recent experimental and computational studies demonstrated the
presence of advective transport of solutes within the RO membrane 9,20,21. Correspondingly, advanced models
conceptualizing water and solute transport through porous RO membranes were developed, incorporating more
detailed mechanisms, including Donnan steric partitioning and advective solution friction 22,23. They have shown
improved performance in simulating and fitting data for inert salt ions 24,25. By introducing the fast acid–base
reaction assumption, this modeling framework allows the inclusion of amphoteric ions. Purely simulated results of
pH variation in RO showed the possible feasibility of this modeling framework 26. By adjusting multiple fitting
parameters, reasonable agreement with experiments was achieved when only inert ions and pH were considered 27.
Once additional amphoteric ions (e.g., NH₄⁺) are included, the model’s generalizability declines markedly, and its
predictions of permeate pH, amphoteric ions, and bivalent ions become less reliable even under a single feed pH 28.
The highly coupled and complex equations render the transport of amphoteric ions strongly dependent on the local
membrane pH. For instance, NH₃ transport is governed by the coupled transport of NH₄⁺ and H⁺ 28.

In this study, we propose that the transport of amphoteric ions is governed by uncoupled transport equations of
charged and neutral species, with the solution pH subsequently corrected through equilibrium recalculation. We
analyzed and elucidated the separation and transport of TAN in RO membranes, as well as the complex changes
induced by pH. Based on solute transport theory that considers friction between substances, we developed a
theoretical model, named ammonia partitioning and transport (APT) model, to describe NH /NH + transport in RO
3 4
membranes. This model takes into account diffusion, advection, and electro-migration of solutes, while also
considering the interactions between water, solutes, and the membrane matrix. RO experiments were conducted
under different feed concentrations, pH levels, and operating pressures to validate the model. Our theoretical and
experimental observations reveal the changes in TAN removal performance resulting from the pH-dependent shifts
NH /NH + speciation and RO membrane surface charge, as well as the differences in NH /NH + transmembrane
3 4 3 4
transport behavior, and extend the applicability of the solution-friction model in describing TAN transport in RO
membranes.

Impact of pH value on TAN transport
Although previous studies have observed a significant effect of pH on TAN rejection in RO 11,33, no fundamental
explanation has been provided yet. The APT model enables a quantitative description of TAN transport across the
RO membrane, demonstrating a great fitting performance with an R² of 0.956 for TAN permeability (Figure 2b)
and 0.988 for TAN rejection (Figure 2c). The influence of pH values on TAN transport was examined using a bench-
scale RO at a crossflow velocity of 6.2 mm s–1, an operating hydraulic pressure of 10 bar, a feed TAN concentration
of 10.7 mM, and a temperature of 25 ± 1 °C.
We observed stable water permeability independent of feed pH variations. As illustrated in Figure 2a, both
experimental results (0.539  0.019 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) and model calculations (0.554 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) demonstrate a
stable water transport coefficient across the tested feed pH range (5.5 to 11). This is probably because water
transport primarily depends on the frictional interaction between water molecules and the membrane 24. Although
the water transport is theoretically coupled with ion transport, the ion-associated term in Eq. 3 is negligible in dilute
solutions. Therefore, observable changes in water permeability only occur when the membrane properties are
significantly altered, such as by swelling under extreme pH conditions 34 or compaction under excessively high
pressure 35.
TAN permeability coefficient initially decreases slightly as feed pH increases, followed by a sharp increase
when the pH exceeds 8 (Figure 2b). The model results indicate that the lowest permeability coefficient occurs at
pH 7.3, with a value of 0.656 L m⁻² h⁻¹. Correspondingly, TAN rejection exhibits a parabolic trend (Figure 2c),
with the highest experimental rejection of 89.13.2% observed near pH 7 and a model-predicted maximum of 88.7%
at pH 7.3. Both high and low pH levels in the feed solution led to a reduced TAN rejection efficiency. This arch-
shaped behavior has also been reported in previous studies 11,36. To better understand the arch-shape, we use the
APT model to separate the pH-dependent transport behavior of TAN into individual transport characteristics of
NH₃ and NH₄⁺.

Model development
The commercial RO membranes typically use the thin-film composite polyamide membranes produced through
interfacial polymerization 42. The model in this study describes the membrane layer as a polymer network with
continuous, water-filled sub-nanometer channels through which clusters of water molecules and solutes can move
24. The support layer also has a similar polymer network, but with much larger voids, and thus, its effect on water
and solute transport can be neglected during model development, allowing us to focus only on the active layer of
the membrane. In the polymer matrix of the membrane, water exists in a liquid phase, while solutes are dispersed
in the water and transported across the membrane through the aqueous phase.

relationship through dissociation equilibrium at every local point inside the membrane 28. However, such method
cannot describe the transport mechanism of NH as its concentration was calculated based on the transport of NH +

Equation solving and parameter fitting procedure
The model is solved analytically following a structured two-loop procedure. The outer loop iterates over
experimental conditions investigated in this study, including feed pH, solute concentration, or permeate flux. Under
each fixed condition, an inner loop determines whether the concentration polarization condition (Eq. 6) is satisfied.
At the beginning of each iteration, the solute concentration at the membrane surface is assumed equal to that in the
feed (i.e., c = c , no polarization).

At the feed-side membrane-water interface, the Donnan-steric partition equations (Eqs. 1.1 and 1.2), together
with the electroneutrality condition inside the membrane (Eqs. 8 and 10), form a solvable system that yields the
solute concentrations and the dimensionless potential difference (∆𝜑 ) at the interface. Within the membrane,
transport equations (Eqs. 2.1 and 2.2) are constructed, which, together with Eqs. (7) (8) and (10), form another
solvable system. This system yields the concentrations and potential difference at the permeate-side interior of the
membrane. At the permeate-side membrane-water interface, the Donnan-steric equilibrium conditions (Eqs. 1.1 and
1.2), coupled with Eqs. (8) (9) and (10), provide analytical solutions for the permeate concentrations of all solutes.

## Introduction

Ammonia is essential to securing the food supply and supporting global population growth. Synthesized by the
Haber-Bosch process, ammonia has sustained about half of humanity over the past century 1. Currently, the Haber-
Bosch process accounts for 2% of global energy consumption and up to 5% of global greenhouse gas emissions 2-
4. This ammonia is consumed and cycled within the food chain and ends up in the excreta. In the U.S., 60% of
ammonia emissions are attributed to the livestock manure wastewater produced in intensive animal feeding
operations 5. Excess manure nutrients lead to overapplication, increasing nutrient losses and reducing nutrient use
efficiency. The high water content and low nutrient density increase costs to transport manure nutrients to cropland,
with agronomic needs restricting the ability to use manure effectively.

Ammonia in manure can be directly reused through a shortcut resource recovery process 6,7. To achieve clean
water that meets discharge or even drinking standards, anaerobic treatment is applied to livestock manure, followed
by a series of membrane treatment processes 8, to recover energy, nutrients, and clean water out of waste streams.
As the dominant technology for water purification with high energy efficiency, reverse osmosis (RO) is increasingly
used for wastewater reclamation 9, particularly for clean water recovery and ammonia concentration 10,11. Compared
with treating the wastewater by nitrification-denitrification and resynthesizing ammonia from the Haber-Bosch
process, this shortcut was estimated to save energy as high as 16.2-19.7 kWh per kg-N 11, making it a more
sustainable solution 12-14.

In practice, it has been found that total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is difficult to fully retain in a single-pass RO,
and thus, a two-pass RO system is often employed to minimize the presence of TAN in the final clean water. Recent
studies reported experimental observation of significant variability in ammonia retention efficiency by RO
membranes, ranging from 0% to 98% 10,11,15,16. These results are particularly sensitive to the operating pH 11. It is
commonly believed that this variability results from the NH /NH + speciation under varying pH, and NH and NH +
3 4 3 4
have their respective permeabilities, which are different from each other. RO membrane is effective for only
rejecting the charged ions, so a high permeability of TAN was observed at alkaline pH, where TAN is mainly in the
form of NH 10,17. However, even at acidic pH where all the TAN exists in the form of NH +,
3 4
its permeability is not
simply a constant due to its interaction with the membrane charge 11. Current understandings are limited to
experimental observations and qualitative descriptions. A fundamental understanding of TAN transport through RO
membranes remains limited; thus, a quantitative model is needed to establish the relation between TAN transport
and pH variation.

Researchers have made significant efforts to develop models to describe the transport of water and salts through
RO membranes 18,19 (Supplementary Table 1). Recent experimental and computational studies demonstrated the
presence of advective transport of solutes within the RO membrane 9,20,21. Correspondingly, advanced models
conceptualizing water and solute transport through porous RO membranes were developed, incorporating more
detailed mechanisms, including Donnan steric partitioning and advective solution friction 22,23. They have shown

reaction assumption, this modeling framework allows the inclusion of amphoteric ions. Purely simulated results of

Model development
The commercial RO membranes typically use the thin-film composite polyamide membranes produced through
interfacial polymerization 42. The model in this study describes the membrane layer as a polymer network with
continuous, water-filled sub-nanometer channels through which clusters of water molecules and solutes can move
24. The support layer also has a similar polymer network, but with much larger voids, and thus, its effect on water
and solute transport can be neglected during model development, allowing us to focus only on the active layer of

Equation solving and parameter fitting procedure
The model is solved analytically following a structured two-loop procedure. The outer loop iterates over
experimental conditions investigated in this study, including feed pH, solute concentration, or permeate flux. Under
each fixed condition, an inner loop determines whether the concentration polarization condition (Eq. 6) is satisfied.
At the beginning of each iteration, the solute concentration at the membrane surface is assumed equal to that in the
feed (i.e., c = c , no polarization).
s f
At the feed-side membrane-water interface, the Donnan-steric partition equations (Eqs. 1.1 and 1.2), together
with the electroneutrality condition inside the membrane (Eqs. 8 and 10), form a solvable system that yields the
solute concentrations and the dimensionless potential difference (∆𝜑 ) at the interface. Within the membrane,
transport equations (Eqs. 2.1 and 2.2) are constructed, which, together with Eqs. (7) (8) and (10), form another
solvable system. This system yields the concentrations and potential difference at the permeate-side interior of the
membrane. At the permeate-side membrane-water interface, the Donnan-steric equilibrium conditions (Eqs. 1.1 and
1.2), coupled with Eqs. (8) (9) and (10), provide analytical solutions for the permeate concentrations of all solutes.
The resulting permeate concentrations (c ) are then substituted back into Eq. (6) to compute the membrane
p
surface concentrations that satisfy the concentration polarization condition. If the updated values differ from the
initial guess, the membrane-surface concentrations are updated by averaging the new and old values; the process
iterates until concentrations at the feed, membrane surface, and permeate simultaneously satisfy Eq. (6). At
convergence, the solution set satisfies all coupled relationships, including concentration polarization, Donnan and
steric partitioning, and Nernst–Planck transport. Because NH₃ and NH₄⁺ exhibit different permeabilities, they must
reestablish chemical equilibrium via Eq. (5), which determines the permeate pH. After obtaining solute
concentrations and fluxes, the pressure drop across the membrane is determined through Eqs. (3), (13), and (14).
Parameter fitting was performed by minimizing the discrepancies between measured and calculated values. The
partitioning coefficients were fitted by minimizing the sum of squared errors between measured and predicted TAN
permeability coefficient and the rejection, with a weighing factor to adjust their magnitude to be the same level,
while the fluid–membrane friction parameter was fitted using water permeability measurements. Optimization was
conducted in MATLAB using the ‘fminsearch’ function (Nelder–Mead algorithm). To enhance convergence and
reduce the likelihood of local minima, the partitioning coefficients were constrained to the literature-based range
of 0–0.2 24,28, and the friction parameter was searched within a logarithmic range of 1013–1017. A multi-start strategy
(n = 4) was applied to further reduce the risk of local minima. Minor manual adjustments were applied to ensure a
consistent parameter set across multiple operating conditions (e.g., varying feed pH, operating pressures, and feed
concentrations; Supplementary Figures 1–2). A complete list of parameter values and their origins (literature-based,
experimentally determined, or fitted) is provided in Supplementary Table 2.

RO Setup and Experiments
A bench-scale crossflow RO system (Innovator CF016, Sterlitech Corporation, Auburn, WA) was employed to
carry out the RO experiment. The system featured a rectangular plate-and-frame feed flow channel with dimensions
of 5.3 cm in length, 3.9 cm in width, and 0.23 cm in depth, giving it an active membrane area of 20.6 cm2. A porous
stainless-steel frit provided mechanical support on the permeate side.
All experiments were conducted at 25 ± 1°C, with a crossflow velocity of 6.2 mm s⁻¹ at the membrane surface.
The retentate was recirculated back to the feed tank, and experiments were conducted across a range of operating
pressures from 5 to 20 bar, feed TAN concentrations from 50 to 1270 mg N/L, and feed pH values from 5.5 to 10.5
to determine TAN rejection rates and permeate flux. The feed volume for each experimental condition was 2 L.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript described an ammonia nitrogen partitioning and transport (ANPT) model to predict NH3/NH4+ transport in RO membranes. This model seems to be useful framework for predicting the transport and rejection of NH3/NH4+ in RO membrane, which is important study for resource recovery. However, the operating conditions examined in this paper appear to be at a gap with regard to their application towards the intended ammonia recovery and reuse. Is this model unable to deal with the 2nd RO shown in Fig. 5a? Consequently, these other ions appear to exert negligible influence on the model, likely contributing to the good fitting results observed in Fig. 5. What effects might be expected on this model under conditions where other ion concentrations are high? Such investigations are thought to yield good predictions for actual wastewater.
3. In the MD simulation of Fig.4, the authors mentioned that “adsorption of NH4+ is mainly dictated by electrostatic attraction with the polyamide membrane, while NH3 is not.” Please compare the extent to which electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding, and van der Waals forces influence the interaction between NH₄⁺ or NH₃ with polyamide membranes.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript develops an Ammonia Nitrogen Partitioning and Transport (ANPT) model for RO that couples steric, Donnan, dielectric partitioning at the interfaces with extended Nernst-Planck/Maxwell-Stefan transport inside the membrane, and explicitly treats NH3 and NH4+ as separate species with re‑equilibration in the permeate.
